title: Mathlib Imports
content: Imports Mathlib's SimpleGraph (adjacency, cliques), Finset basics, binomial coefficients (Nat.Choose), and general tactics. SimpleGraph.Clique provides the clique predicate used in the Ramsey number definition, while Nat.Choose gives $\binom{n}{2}$ for the edge decomposition.
mathContext: Requires $\text{SimpleGraph}$, $\text{Finset.card}$, $\text{Nat.choose}$ for graph structure, edge counting, and the binomial decomposition $m = \binom{n}{2} + t$.

title: Edge Count and No Isolated Vertices
content: edgeCount G computes $|E(G)|$ as the cardinality of the edge finset. NoIsolatedVertices G requires every vertex to have at least one neighbor. Both are needed to state the problem: the conjecture concerns graphs with exactly $m$ edges and no isolated vertices, since isolated vertices don't affect the Ramsey number but inflate the vertex count.

title: Edge Colorings and Monochromatic Cliques
content: EdgeColoring n is a function $\text{Fin}\,n \to \text{Fin}\,n \to \text{Bool}$ representing a 2-coloring of $K_n$'s edges. IsValidColoring requires symmetry ($c(i,j) = c(j,i)$) and irreflexivity ($c(i,i) = \text{false}$). IsMonochromaticClique c S b holds when all edges within $S$ have color $b$. These definitions set up the combinatorial framework for Ramsey theory: we seek monochromatic structures in arbitrary 2-colorings.
mathContext: $c : \text{Fin}\,n \times \text{Fin}\,n \to \{0,1\}$ with $c(i,j) = c(j,i)$ and $c(i,i) = 0$; $\text{MonoClique}(c, S, b) \iff \forall i \neq j \in S,\; c(i,j) = b$

title: Ramsey Numbers $R(k)$ and $R(G)$
content: ramseyNumber k is $R(k)$, the minimum $n$ such that every valid 2-coloring of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic $K_k$. Defined via Nat.find with an existence witness $2^k$ (sorry). ramseyNumberGraph G generalizes to arbitrary graphs: the minimum $n$ such that every 2-coloring of $K_n$ contains a monochromatic copy of $G$. The graph version has a definition sorry since formalizing graph homomorphisms requires substantial infrastructure.
mathContext: $R(k) = \min\{n : \forall c \text{ valid 2-coloring of } K_n,\; \exists S \subseteq V,\; |S| = k,\; S \text{ monochromatic}\}$; $R(G) = \min\{n : \forall c,\; K_n \supseteq \text{mono copy of } G\}$

title: Maximally Complete Graph and the Erdos-Graham Conjecture
content: The edge decomposition writes $m = \binom{n}{2} + t$ with $0 \leq t < n$: the unique way to express $m$ edges as a complete graph $K_n$ plus $t$ extra edges. The maximally complete graph $H_m$ is $K_n$ with a new vertex connected to $t$ vertices of $K_n$, i.e., $K_n \vee \overline{K_t}$ (join with an independent set). The Erdos-Graham conjecture states $R(G) \leq R(H_m)$ for all $m$-edge graphs $G$ without isolated vertices. decomposeEdges and maximallyCompleteGraph both have sorries due to the non-trivial construction.
mathContext: $m = \binom{n}{2} + t,\; 0 \leq t < n$; $H_m = K_n + K_{1,t}$; conjecture: $\forall G$ with $|E(G)| = m,\; R(G) \leq R(H_m)$

title: Counterexamples and the Asymptotic Conjecture
content: The conjecture fails for $m \in \{2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9\}$ — for these edge counts, there exist graphs $G$ with $R(G) > R(H_m)$. Note the gap: $m = 6 = \binom{4}{2}$ (a complete graph) is not a counterexample, consistent with the idea that 'complete-like' graphs are the hardest. The axiom counterexamples_exist formalizes this. The corrected asymptotic conjecture ErdosGrahamConjectureAsymptotic posits $\exists M$ such that the inequality holds for all $m \geq M$. This remains open — even the existence of such an $M$ is unknown.
mathContext: $\forall m \in \{2,3,4,5,7,8,9\},\; \exists G,\; |E(G)| = m \wedge R(G) > R(H_m)$; asymptotic: $\exists M,\; \forall m \geq M,\; \forall G,\; R(G) \leq R(H_m)$

title: Sudakov's Upper Bound (2011)
content: Benny Sudakov proved that $R(G) \leq 2^{C\sqrt{m}}$ for some absolute constant $C > 0$ and any graph $G$ with $m$ edges. This is weaker than the Erdos-Graham conjecture (which would give $R(G) \leq R(H_m)$, with $R(H_m)$ depending on the specific structure of $H_m$) but holds universally. The proof uses the dependent random choice technique combined with the Kovari-Sos-Turan theorem. This theorem has a sorry.
mathContext: $\exists C > 0,\; \forall G \text{ with } m \text{ edges},\; R(G) \leq 2^{C\sqrt{m}}$

title: Classical Ramsey Numbers and Bounds
content: The file records four classical Ramsey values: $R(1) = 1$ (trivial), $R(2) = 2$ (any edge is monochromatic), $R(3) = 6$ (the party problem — any 2-coloring of $K_6$ contains a monochromatic triangle), and $R(4) = 18$ (Greenwood-Gleason 1955). Two quantitative bounds follow: the probabilistic lower bound $R(k) \geq 2^{k/2}$ (Erdos 1947, the first application of the probabilistic method) and the pigeonhole upper bound $R(k) \leq 4^k$ (from the recurrence $R(k) \leq 2R(k-1)$). All have sorries.

title: Edge Monotonicity and Subgraph Bounds
content: Two monotonicity results: (1) if $G \subseteq H$ (same vertex set, $G$'s edges are a subset of $H$'s), then $R(G) \leq R(H)$, since any monochromatic copy of $H$ contains a monochromatic copy of $G$; (2) if $G$ is isomorphic to a subgraph of $H$, then $R(G) \leq R(H)$, by composing the embedding with the containment. These are fundamental properties that underpin the Erdos-Graham conjecture: it asks which specific graph maximizes $R(G)$ for a given edge count. Both have sorries.
mathContext: $G \subseteq H \implies R(G) \leq R(H)$; $G \hookrightarrow H \implies R(G) \leq R(H)$
